_README: Human adjudications that settle a queued ruling. The other half of rejections.json:
that file records 'do not publish', this one records 'a person read this and it is
fine'. Without it the review queue cannot shrink -- verify.py re-surfaces every
medium-confidence and flagged item on every run, so the same items get re-read forever
and the queue stops meaning anything.
An approval is scoped to the exact text and sources it was given. `signature` is
verify.py's fingerprint of (ruling text + cited comment ids + thread context) at review
time; if any of those change the approval lapses and the item returns to the queue. So
an approval cannot silence a ruling that was later rewritten, which is the whole risk of
a file like this.
Write `signature: null` to approve regardless of future edits. Do that only for a
finding about the *source* rather than the ruling -- e.g. 'this answer is terse because
the question carried the polarity, and that is correct here'.
verdict is one of:
approved   the ruling is faithful and well-sourced; the model's objection is wrong or moot
accepted   the objection is fair but the ruling is the best available; reason says why
A ruling that should change is not recorded here -- change it. A ruling that should go
is not recorded here either -- that is rejections.json.
The 30 `terse source` approvals dated 2026-08-30 all rest on the same evidence, and the
reason quotes it: the question the terse answer was replying to, recovered by walking
`parent` up the comment thread. A short answer's polarity lives in its question, so that
quote is the whole check -- read it against the ruling and the approval either holds or
it does not. Three items in that pass were not approved; the rulings were changed.
The 38 approvals dated 2026-08-31 clear the medium-confidence and qualified-answer
queues. Each was read against the whole comment thread rather than the cited comment,
because both queues are about scope, not polarity: a medium verdict usually means the
rule was transferred to a card the thread did not name, and a qualified verdict means
the official answer carried a caveat. So the reason for each says which comment licenses
which clause, and -- for a transfer -- why the unnamed card is covered. Four items were
not approved as they stood: two omnibus rows were split (20201104, 20260208), one hedge
was restored (20260128) and one addition was rewritten as a consequence (20190311).
The 3 approvals for the batch-7 transfers are medium for the reason every transfer is:
the thread named the sibling card. Each reason says which power makes the two cards
interchangeable, and -- for 20201010b, whose source is 15 characters long -- which
question fixes the direction of the yes.

reason: Approved as rewritten. Source is Jamey relaying David Studley: "The answer is 3. You draw 3,
keep 2. The Automa gets nothing, as usual." The row now derives the third card's discard
from the Automa getting nothing instead of asserting it. Kept even though it is a solo-mode

answers that question in that direction.

The verifier holds this at `overstated`/medium on the grounds that Jamey hedged twice
and never himself determined whether Spangled Drongo's power is scoped to the 'gain
food' action, so the ruling's flat 'by any means' clause is stronger than comment 42903
supports. That objection is accurate about 42903 and moot about the corpus: comment
109108 answers exactly that question ('does this mean that during a round a player gains
a nectar for any reason - not just gaining food' / 'it does mean what you described'),
and is listed in extra-citations.json. The verifier itself concedes the conclusion is
defensible on that basis.
Its remaining objection -- that 109108's once-between-turns point is dropped -- is
correct but not a defect here. That limit is published on Spangled Drongo's own card as
ruling 20241228. A player reading Red-Winged Parrot needs to know that a gift counts as
a gain; they do not need the Drongo's timing rule on the Parrot's page.
Keeping the verdict rather than forcing it to faithful: the model is reasoning correctly
from what it was given, and loosening the gate to make one item green would cost the
next inversion.

hummingbird spaces are full you attract none" is the asker's own framing -- "does this mean
you must have two clear rows... and if full you cant attract any" -- which Jamey answered by
restricting the power to open spaces.
"You'll just gain at most 1 food token from this power" answers "do you get to choose one of
the two or do you get both from the supply?" Ruling out both leaves choosing, so the row's
"choose which one" is the other half of the same answer rather than an addition.
Ordering from 151259 verbatim ("The egg laying happens last, after you've finished playing
the other bird (including it's "when played" power, if any)"); the Red Kite case from
151361, "I would say yes, the egg laying still takes place." The row states it flatly. "I
would say" is a politeness marker, not a stated qualification -- unlike "at least for now"
or "as long as you're consistent with your group", which are limits or permissions a player
needs and which this review restores wherever they were dropped.
Graham Sadie asked: “Does the Orinoco goose's power include neighbouring nests of star type
as well as box nests?”  Jamey Stegmaier answered: “It does!”  The ruling answers that
question in that direction.
The cited 165106 is Jamey's answer after Patricia identified the card, and it reverses the
general guess he had offered in 165088 before seeing it ("It seems to me that both of these
situations would let you gain the seeds, reset, then cache the rodent"). The later, card-
specific answer is the ruling, on the newer-and-more-specific-wins precedent. Hedged in
wording only ("The way I read this particular card... I would not say"), which the row
states flatly -- the same reading of hedges as 20260324.
